evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: paleography; oracle-bone forms and early use
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 火 as an oracle-bone picture of rising flames and says its original meaning is fire. It notes that 火 forms can be confused with 山, that the dots are not always present, and that inscriptions help distinguish them. It reports no bronze-inscription form in its collection and describes Warring States forms as linearized, with an upturned stroke reversed and a horizontal added to the vertical. It cites oracle-bone examples: 合集30774 火不延 in the literal fire sense; 合集11503 for the star name 大火; and 合集34797 旬亡火, interpreted by some as a phonetic loan for 禍 ‘calamity’ because the words were close in sound. The loan interpretation is attributed to Chen Weizhan, not presented as certain.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — oracle-bone component 火

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, reproducing 說文解字 and 段玉裁注
evidence.text: The transmitted Shuowen entry says 火 is 燬, associates it with the southern phase, describes flames rising, calls it a pictogram, and says fire-related characters use it. Duan Yucai corrects 燬 to 𤈦 by comparison with a later Shuowen entry and describes the graph as broad below and pointed above. This is a Han-period lexicographic account, not independent proof of the Shang graphic origin.
evidence.title: 說文解字「火」 — Shuowen.org

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.text: The dictionary identifies the oracle-bone use in 合集11503, 㞢新大星並火, as 火 referring to the star 大火, identified there with Antares / 心宿二. It separately cites 詩經·豳風·七月 七月流火 as a later literary example of 火 as a short name for that star. This supports a distinct star-name use but does not establish when or by what semantic path the star acquired that name.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — oracle-bone component 火

evidence.source: Sagart and Ma, Zenodo record for their 2020 article
evidence.field: Old Chinese vocabulary methodology and dating scope
evidence.text: The authors say their list uses the Baxter–Sagart 2014 Old Chinese reconstruction and selects Chinese words attested before the Han period using meanings from major lexica. They retain multiple candidate words where it is unclear which is oldest. The accessible record does not expose a 火-specific entry in its text, so it does not independently establish 火's reconstruction or cognacy.
evidence.title: A 250-item list of Old Chinese vocabulary in the Baxter-Sagart reconstruction

evidence.field: Old Chinese reconstruction data; local TSV cross-check
evidence.text: The repository row for 火 is: huǒ; Middle Chinese xwaX; Old Chinese *[qʷʰ]ˤəjʔ; gloss fire; GSR 0353a. This differs substantially from the separate Wiktionary account of a 2024 proposal *X.pˤərʔ. These are different reconstructions/analyses and must not be merged or silently normalized. The externally opened Baxter–Sagart supplementary site describes its downloadable lists as accompanying Old Chinese: a new reconstruction (2014), but the linked PDF fetch failed, so the exact row above is verified from the local structured TSV as instructed, not from a successfully opened external table.
evidence.title: The Baxter-Sagart reconstruction of Old Chinese

evidence.text: The entry reports Zhengzhang Shangfang's Old Chinese *qʰʷaːlʔ and cites a proposed 2024 Baxter–Sagart update *X.pˤərʔ, relating it to 燹 and proposing broader cognacy with PTB *par and Proto-Austronesian *dapuʀ. It also mentions a possible PTB *məj comparison and flags phonological problems. These are secondary-source summaries of disputed comparative proposals; the pages inspected do not supply enough primary comparative evidence to adjudicate them. The local Baxter–Sagart TSV instead has *[qʷʰ]ˤəjʔ for 火.
evidence.title: 火 — Wiktionary

evidence.text: The inspected reconstruction entry describes Proto-Tibeto-Burman *mey and Proto-Sino-Tibetan variants *myəy ~ sməy/smyəy, but explicitly says comparison with Chinese 火 huǒ is problematic. It summarizes earlier proposals and competing reconstructions; this makes inherited cognacy uncertain and prevents treating the similarity as settled etymology.
evidence.title: Reconstruction:Proto-Sino-Tibetan/məj — Wiktionary

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, reproducing 說文解字 and 段玉裁注
evidence.text: The entry gives 呼果切 for 火 and reproduces the Shuowen explanation. This supplies a traditional fanqie, not by itself a reconstructed Middle Chinese pronunciation. The local TSV and Wiktionary give xwaX in Baxter's Middle Chinese notation; their notation and the fanqie tradition should remain distinct.
evidence.title: 說文解字「火」 — Shuowen.org

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.text: 火 is analyzed as a standalone pictograph, not as a compound with a semantic or phonetic subcomponent. In related graphs, the entry says 光 includes 火 with 卩, 赤 includes 大 with 火, and 炎 repeats 火 twice. Those are analyses of those separate graphs; they do not make 火 a sound component in 火 itself.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — oracle-bone component 火

gaps: No component-specific phonetic element exists in the graph 火; it is analyzed as a pictograph. Modern Mandarin huǒ is given by Wiktionary; Cantonese fo2 is also listed there. No primary modern pronunciation reference was opened.

The accessible paleographic lexicon supplies inscription numbers but not dated archaeological provenience for each inscription. Oracle-bone evidence is Shang-period, but no narrower date for the cited 火 tokens was established here.
The university lexicon reports 火 not found in bronze inscriptions in its collection; this is a collection-specific absence, not proof that no bronze instance exists anywhere.
The star-name usage is attested in oracle-bone material and later in the Classic of Poetry, but the semantic motivation for naming the star 大火/火 is not established by inspected evidence.

The interpretation of 合集34797 as a loan for 禍 is attributed to a scholar and based on sound proximity and contextual reading; the precise phonological comparison and alternative readings were not independently checked.
A whole-graph phonetic loan does not apply to the graphic origin. No independently sourced early name/pronunciation for a depicted object is needed for the pictographic fire analysis.

External retrieval of the Baxter–Sagart PDF returned 502. The local TSV row was checked exactly and retained as *[qʷʰ]ˤəjʔ, Middle Chinese xwaX. The 2024 *X.pˤərʔ proposal remains secondary-reported and is not verified against the primary paper.

PTB *par and Proto-Austronesian *dapuʀ cognacy claims, and the proposed 2024 relationship with 燹, were not established from opened primary comparative datasets. Treat these as disputed/unverified proposals rather than settled origins.
The repository glosses anger/rage and burn were not dated or linked historically to the primary sense in inspected external sources; no chronology is inferred from those glosses.
No glyph images were visually inspected, so the shape description is reported from the scholarly text rather than independent visual examination.
